sections.heading: Longing for the day when help gives way to home
sections.text: My Lord, bring me safely to the place where I will not need the supports I need now. I will not need fasting, urgent praying, tears, watchfulness, preaching, or the Lord’s Supper the way I need them here, because I will finally be with you face to face. I will not be fighting temptation anymore. Nothing unclean will get in. Nothing will spoil love, worship, or joy.
theological_themes: Heaven is the fulfillment toward which the ordinary means of grace point. In glory, faith gives way to sight, temptation ends, and communion with God is immediate and unhindered.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts the partial, indirect knowledge believers have now with the face-to-face knowledge to come. This supports the prayer’s longing for the day when present helps are surpassed by direct communion with God.
John’s vision of the new Jerusalem makes clear that nothing unclean enters God’s final dwelling place. That grounds the prayer’s hope for a world where nothing defiles or corrupts worship.

sections.heading: Hoping for a world without sorrow or decay
sections.text: I long for the place where grief, sin, death, distance, and tears are gone. No more pale faces, failing bodies, aching joints, helpless weakness, old age worn down by decay, hidden disease, exhausting fear, or anxious care. No more bodies breaking down. No more hearts being crushed. Make me ready for the life where I will be whole before you.
theological_themes: The new creation removes the curse’s effects: death, mourning, pain, bodily weakness, fear, and separation. Christian hope includes the restoration of the whole person, body and soul.

scripture_references.connection: This passage describes God dwelling with his people and wiping away every tear, with death, mourning, crying, and pain gone. It directly grounds the prayer’s longing for heaven as the end of sorrow and separation.
Paul teaches that the resurrection body is raised imperishable, glorious, powerful, and spiritual. This supports the prayer’s hope that bodily frailty and decay will not have the last word.

sections.heading: Wanting every desire to be made whole in you
sections.text: There, everything in me will finally work the way it was made to work. The clearer my sight, the more beautiful you will be to me. The purer my hunger, the sweeter your goodness will taste. The more tuned my heart becomes, the more deeply I will rejoice in your praise. The more complete you make my soul, the more fully I will enjoy you. Most of all, I will know you without the fog that clouds me now.
theological_themes: Glorification perfects human faculties so that the believer can know, love, worship, and enjoy God without the distortions of sin. Heaven is not merely escape from pain but fullness of delight in God himself.

scripture_references.connection: John says believers do not yet fully see what they will be, but when Christ appears they will be like him because they will see him as he is. This connects perfected sight of God with the believer’s transformation.
David describes fullness of joy in God’s presence and lasting pleasures with him. This supports the prayer’s view that heaven’s deepest happiness is the enjoyment of God himself.

sections.heading: Admitting how little I understand now
sections.text: Here, Lord, I am so small. I can observe your world, and I can think about you, but I cannot take you in. Compared with you, I am like a tiny creature trying to understand a human mind. I know truly what you have revealed, but not clearly or completely. Keep me humble about what I do not know, and keep me trusting you until sight replaces faith.
theological_themes: Creaturely limitation remains even in true faith. God is knowable because he reveals himself, but he is never exhaustively comprehended by finite creatures in this life.

scripture_references.connection: God declares that his thoughts and ways are higher than ours. This supports the prayer’s humble admission that present understanding of God is real but limited.

Moses distinguishes between the secret things belonging to God and the revealed things given to his people. This helps preserve the prayer’s balance: God is truly known through revelation, yet not fully grasped.

sections.heading: Looking forward to being with you and your people
sections.text: But there I will be near you. I will live with your family. I will stand in your royal presence, not as an outsider but as an heir of your kingdom. I will belong fully to Christ—joined to him, loved by him, and sharing in the life he has with you. With body and soul made new, I will use every part of myself to enjoy you forever.
theological_themes: The believer’s hope is nearness to God, fellowship with God’s household, inheritance in the kingdom, and union with Christ. The final state is embodied, relational, and centered on communion with God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul links adoption, being God’s children, and becoming heirs with Christ. This supports the prayer’s confidence that the believer will stand before God not as a stranger but as a welcomed heir.
Paul presents marriage as a mystery pointing to Christ and the church. This grounds the prayer’s bridal language in Scripture while keeping Christ’s covenant love at the center.
The final vision shows God’s servants worshiping him, seeing his face, and reigning with him. This supports the hope of near, embodied, eternal service and enjoyment in God’s presence.

sections.heading: Learning now the praise I will offer forever
sections.text: Since praise is fitting for your people, teach me to practice it now. Let praise shape the way I pray, read your Word, listen, work, and notice what is in front of me. Let me honor you when others are watching and when enemies oppose me. Train my heart and mouth now for the worship I hope to give you forever.
theological_themes: Present worship is preparation for eternal worship. Praise is not confined to formal prayer but belongs in the whole life of the believer, including public witness and opposition.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm calls the righteous to rejoice in the Lord because praise is fitting for them. This directly supports the prayer’s desire to learn praise as the proper language of God’s people.
Hebrews describes continual praise through Christ as a sacrifice offered to God. This grounds the request that praise mark ordinary life now, not only future worship in heaven.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The line about the “means of grace” ceasing could sound dismissive of prayer, preaching, fasting, and sacraments. I rendered it as longing for their fulfilled purpose in direct communion with God, not as contempt for them in the present life.

The original uses bridal language for the believer in relation to Christ. Because Scripture primarily applies this image to the church corporately, I kept the idea but phrased it as personal belonging to Christ within his covenant love rather than making an overly individualized romantic image central.

The original’s detailed references to bodily decline reflect older medical language and assumptions. I preserved the concrete focus on sickness, aging, fear, and decay while avoiding obsolete terms like “peccant humours.”
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “dwell with my family” as dwelling with God’s family, the household of the redeemed, rather than specifically with one’s earthly relatives, since the surrounding lines focus on kingdom, inheritance, and union with Christ.

I kept the ant image as an admission of creaturely smallness before God, but clarified that the believer can still know truly what God reveals. This avoids implying that God is unknowable in a skeptical sense.

I treated “personal completeness” as the final perfection of the whole person—body and soul—in resurrection life, because the prayer links it with bodily weakness, perfected perception, and the enjoyment of God.
